b: Search intent is the goal a person has when typing a query into a search engine: to learn something, to reach a particular website, to compare options or to complete a purchase. The words of a query are only a proxy for that goal. "Jaguar" may be a car, an animal or a football club; "running shoes" may come from a researcher or from someone with a card in hand. The concept exists because search engines and advertisers both need to infer what a person wants from a handful of words, and because the right answer to a query depends far more on its purpose than on its vocabulary.

For marketers, intent decides which pages rank, which ads are eligible to appear, what a click is worth and, increasingly, which queries an automated system treats as equivalent to a keyword the advertiser chose.

The vocabulary dates to Andrei Broder, then at AltaVista. His paper "A taxonomy of web search", published in SIGIR Forum (volume 36, issue 2) in the autumn of 2002, divided searches into three classes by immediate goal. In an informational query the intent is "to acquire some information assumed to be present on one or more web pages"; in a navigational query "the immediate intent is to reach a particular site"; and in a transactional query the intent is "to perform some web-mediated activity", such as shopping or downloading.

Broder's evidence came from AltaVista users. A pop-up survey run between June 26 and November 3, 2001 produced 3,190 valid responses, 24.5% of them navigational. A manual review of 400 logged queries put informational at 48%, transactional at 30% and navigational at 20%. Broder himself called the log figures "very 'soft'", because intent has to be guessed from a few words.

Later studies moved the numbers. In April 2008, Bernard Jansen, Danielle Booth and Amanda Spink ran an automatic classifier over more than 1.5 million queries and found about 80% informational and roughly 10% each navigational and transactional.
The SEO industry later added a fourth class, commercial (sometimes called commercial investigation), for queries such as "best CRM for small business" that sit between research and purchase.

Search engines do not ask users what they want. They infer it from the query text, from what earlier users clicked for the same or similar queries, from location and device, and from the shape of the results that satisfied people before.

Google's own systems moved steadily from matching words to modelling meaning. Hummingbird, announced on September 26, 2013, rebuilt the core algorithm to handle longer, conversational queries and was reported to affect about 90% of searches. RankBrain, disclosed to Bloomberg on October 26, 2015, applied machine learning to queries Google had not seen before, a group the company has repeatedly put at about 15% of daily searches, according to Search Engine Land and Search Engine Roundtable.

BERT followed on October 25, 2019. Pandu Nayak, Google Fellow and vice president of Search, wrote that it would help the engine better understand "one in 10 searches in the U.S. in English". His example was "2019 brazil traveler to usa need a visa", where the word "to" decides who is travelling where. Nayak also described the habit the change targeted: people "often use 'keyword-ese,' typing strings of words that they think we'll understand, but aren't actually how they'd naturally ask a question."

Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines, the manual used by contractors who grade results, use different labels. The current edition, dated September 11, 2025 and running to 182 pages, sorts queries into Know (with a Know Simple subtype for short factual answers), Do, Website, Visit-in-person and queries with multiple meanings. Raters then score each result on a Needs Met scale from Fails to Meet to Fully Meets, so a well-written page can still fail if it answers the wrong intent.
How intent works in SEO practice

In search engine optimisation (SEO), intent is usually assigned per keyword. Semrush introduced a Keyword Intent metric in 2021, describing it as data on "the four categories of keyword intent - navigational, informational, transactional, and commercial", assigned "automatically using a machine-learning algorithm", according to its December 1, 2021 product roundup. Semrush's guide, dated November 21, 2024, defines search intent as "a user's main goal when they enter a query into a search engine" and acknowledges that "searches often have overlapping intents", citing "blog platform free" as both informational and commercial.

The working method is to read the results page. If the top results for a query are product listings, Google has decided the intent is transactional, and a long article is unlikely to rank; if they are guides, a category page faces the reverse problem. Practitioners rank this alignment above most other signals. The Zyppy Signal ranking factors survey of 131 SEO practitioners, released on September 9, 2026, rated search intent match as the single strongest of 103 signals, with meta descriptions rated lowest.
How intent works in paid search

In pay-per-click (PPC) advertising, intent is priced. A transactional query such as "buy noise cancelling headphones" usually attracts more bidders and higher cost per click (CPC) than an informational one such as "how do noise cancelling headphones work", because it converts more often. Advertisers have traditionally expressed intent through keyword lists, match types and negative keywords.

Platforms have shifted that control towards their own inference. Google added close variants to exact and phrase match in September 2014, and from September 6, 2018 let exact match serve on queries with the same meaning. Its help page now describes exact match as covering searches with "the same meaning or same intent as the keyword". Broad match goes further, matching queries "related to" the keyword using signals such as landing pages and recent searches. Google announced AI Max for Search campaigns on May 6, 2025, extending matching beyond keywords altogether, and began migrating campaigns that used its broad match setting to AI Max on September 1, 2026.

In December 2025, Ginny Marvin, Google's Ads Liaison, said the company was "increasingly determining relevance by inferred intent", after Brad Geddes of Adalysis documented AI Max traffic attributed to exact and phrase keywords.
Measurement and the size of each intent

Estimates of the intent mix depend on who classifies and how. The Datos and SparkToro State of Search report for the fourth quarter of 2025, released on January 28, 2026, put informational queries at 55% to 63% of US queries in both late 2024 and late 2025, while direct purchase intent stayed below 2%. The continuity in that distribution coincided with the fastest growth in queries of six to nine words. Rand Fishkin, SparkToro's co-founder, said the data could "illuminate the difference in intent between AI 'searchers' and traditional search users." The figures are not comparable with Broder's, whose transactional class counted downloads as well as purchases.

The first criticism is that the categories are porous, and every study draws the boundaries differently. A query such as "iphone 17" may be informational, commercial and navigational at once, and vendor tools often assign several labels to a single keyword. A label describes the majority of searchers, not any individual.

The second is that inference transfers power. When exact match follows "intent" rather than words, the platform decides what the intent is, and the platform also sells the inventory. Google's search terms report, since May 2026, has shown some AI Mode and Lens queries as "the best approximation of the user's intent" rather than the words typed. Michael Hulsmann, founder of SearchSavior, described the consequence for exclusions: "Block a junk query and the same intent reappears under a different reported term next week."

The third concerns AI answers absorbing intent before a click. Semrush found that AI Overviews appeared on 88% of 400 tracked commercial keywords in August 2026, up from 45.75% in September 2025, reaching queries once assumed to be safe from summaries because they signal buying.

Purchase intent. A buyer's likelihood of purchasing, measured by surveys, behaviour or third-party signals across channels. Purchase intent is a property of a person; search intent is a property of a query and can be informational with no purchase in view.

Search term and keyword. A keyword is what the advertiser bids on; a search term is what the user typed. Intent is the interpretation that links them, and it is that interpretation platforms increasingly control.
Navigational query. One of the intent classes, not a synonym. A navigational query seeks a specific site, usually by brand name.

Intent data. In B2B marketing, signals that a company is researching a product category, usually gathered from content consumption across publisher networks. It may include search behaviour but is not limited to it.

AI search has made queries longer and intent more explicit. Liz Reid, Google's head of Search, said in April 2026 that users in AI Mode "tell you the real problem. They don't take their need and translate it into what the computer understands." Queries there run two to three times longer than traditional searches. In an Ads Decoded episode on October 28, 2026, Shivani Mohan, Google's vice president for Search data science and user experience research, said query length "has increased 3x" and that Google wants "to be very attuned to the original user intent" when placing ads.
Inference is also moving before the query. Google Research presented work at EMNLP 2025, covered in January 2026, on small on-device models that extract a user's intent from sequences of screens.

Who: Searchers, whose goals the concept describes; search engines such as Google and Microsoft Bing, which infer intent to rank results and match ads; SEO and PPC practitioners and tool vendors such as Semrush that classify keywords; and researchers led by Andrei Broder, who named the categories.
What: The goal behind a search query, usually classed as informational, navigational, commercial or transactional, or in Google's rater terms as Know, Do, Website and Visit-in-person.

When: Defined in Broder's 2002 paper using 2001 AltaVista data; built into Google's ranking through Hummingbird (2013), RankBrain (2015) and BERT (2019); turned into a keyword metric by SEO tools around 2021; reshaped by AI Max and AI Mode in 2025 and 2026.

Where: On search results pages, in ranking systems and rater guidelines, in keyword research tools, and in the matching and reporting systems of Google Ads, Microsoft Advertising and other search ad platforms.

Why: The same words can carry different goals, and the right result or ad depends on the goal. Intent determines what ranks and what a click costs, and as platforms infer it for advertisers, it has become a point of dispute over control and transparency.
